title: Modes of Operation
body:
A block cipher encrypts exactly one block. [[AES]] takes 128 bits and returns 128 bits, and real
messages are not 128 bits. A **mode of operation** is the rule for chaining the cipher across many
blocks, and it is where most deployment bugs actually happen: the cipher is fine, the mode is
wrong.

## ECB, and why not

Electronic Codebook. Encrypt each block independently under the same key:

$$c_i = E_k(m_i)$$

**Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks.** The cipher is a deterministic
[[Permutation]], so equality survives it, and the structure of the plaintext shows straight
through. The standard demonstration is a bitmap image encrypted with ECB: the colours change and
the picture is still perfectly readable.

It is the same failure as a monoalphabetic cipher in [[Classical Ciphers]], one abstraction level
up. There the unit was a letter and the attack was [[Cryptanalysis|frequency analysis]]; here the
unit is a 16-byte block and the attack is the same idea. **Never use ECB.** The only legitimate use
is encrypting a single block of random data, such as a key.

## CBC

Cipher Block Chaining. XOR each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before
encrypting:

$$c_i = E_k(m_i \oplus c_{i-1}), \qquad c_0 = \text{IV}$$

```
m1        m2        m3
 |         |         |
IV -XOR-> c1 -XOR-> c2 -XOR->
 |         |         |
 E         E         E
 |         |         |
 c1        c2        c3
```

Identical plaintext blocks now encrypt differently, because each depends on everything before it.
Decryption is $m_i = D_k(c_i) \oplus c_{i-1}$.

- The **IV must be random and unpredictable**, not merely unique. A predictable IV breaks CBC under
  chosen-plaintext attack, which is what the BEAST attack on TLS 1.0 exploited.
- **Encryption is inherently serial**; block $i$ needs $c_{i-1}$. Decryption parallelises, because
  every $c_{i-1}$ is already known.
- Needs **padding** to a whole block, and getting padding wrong gives you the padding oracle
  attack: an error message that distinguishes "bad padding" from "bad MAC" lets an attacker decrypt
  the whole message a byte at a time without the key.

## CTR

Counter mode. Encrypt a counter and XOR the result with the plaintext:

$$c_i = m_i \oplus E_k(\text{nonce} \| i)$$

**This turns a block cipher into a [[Stream Cipher]].** The cipher is never applied to the message
at all, only to the counter, so it generates a keystream and the message is XOR-ed with it. All the
stream-cipher rules apply, including the important one: **never reuse a (key, nonce) pair**, or the
keystreams collide and $c_1 \oplus c_2 = m_1 \oplus m_2$.

| | ECB | CBC | CTR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hides repeated blocks | no | yes | yes |
| Encryption parallel | yes | **no** | yes |
| Decryption parallel | yes | yes | yes |
| Random access | yes | read-only | yes |
| Padding needed | yes | yes | **no** |
| Nonce reuse | n/a | weakens | **catastrophic** |

CTR wins on nearly every axis, which is why the modern defaults are built on it.

## Confidentiality is not integrity

Every mode here hides the message and **none of them detects tampering**. In CTR mode an attacker
who knows a plaintext byte can flip any bit of the corresponding ciphertext byte and flip exactly
that plaintext bit; CBC lets them corrupt one block to control the next. Encryption without
authentication is a bug, and it is the single most common one in this material.

The fix is an **authenticated encryption** mode: encrypt, then compute a [[HMAC|MAC]] over the
ciphertext, and refuse to decrypt if the MAC fails. **GCM** (Galois/Counter Mode) is CTR plus a
built-in authenticator, and the "Galois" is literal: the tag is computed by multiplication in
$GF(2^{128})$, a [[Finite Field]] one size up from the one [[AES]] itself uses. That is the same
algebra doing a completely different job, and it is worth noticing that the field structure is
what makes the tag hard to forge.

Encrypt-then-MAC is the right order. MAC-then-encrypt and encrypt-and-MAC have both produced real
attacks.
